passage:
Monday, week one. Vijay wrote one line on the whiteboard: 20 clinics signed up and paying by the last Friday of week six. Aadhya taped a sheet over the old feature wish-list and marked the report date for the advisors in red.
Thursday, week three. Nine clinics had watched a demo and three had paid. A developer asked to start a new settings screen; Vijay pointed at the whiteboard and said it could wait. Aadhya booked another round of calls instead.
Friday, week six. Eleven clinics were paying. Vijay's shoulders dropped, then straightened, and the numbers went to the advisors that same afternoon, short of the target and unedited.

qa.q: How many clinics were paying on the Friday of week six?
qa.a: Eleven clinics were paying.

qa.q: What was Vijay probably feeling when sending the numbers on that Friday?
qa.a: Vijay was probably disappointed but steady: the dropped and then straightened shoulders show the letdown, and sending the unedited numbers on time shows resolve.

qa.q: What different approach could the team try if the calls in week three had gone badly, and why?
qa.a: They could look for the root cause by phoning clinics that declined and asking why, because that would show whether to fix the offer or change direction.

qa.q: How might the advisors see the single target and the fixed report date?
qa.a: The advisors get one clear number on a known day, so they can judge the experiment fairly without guessing how it went. 🙂

grounding: The passage shows a team that sets a short fixed period and one measure, freezes other work and reports on a fixed date.

passage:
Mentor's note, Friday. Rashmi here, writing up the five weeks I sat in on Joseph's team.
Tuesday after the first investor chat, Joseph told everyone to add an AI helper. Two weeks later, after another chat, the plan became fast delivery. Last week, after a third, it turned into a marketplace. Each time, half-built work was put aside.
At the Thursday stand-up one engineer said quietly, "We never finish a test before the next idea arrives." Nobody replied, and two people looked at their laptops.
I asked Joseph what the numbers said about any of the three. There were no numbers, because nothing ran long enough to measure. We agreed to talk again on Monday.

qa.q: Which three ideas did the product swing toward?
qa.a: It swung toward an AI helper, fast delivery and a marketplace.

qa.q: What does the engineer's remark at the stand-up suggest about how the team felt?
qa.a: It suggests the engineer felt frustrated and doubtful, because nothing they built stayed around long enough to be tested.

qa.q: What could Joseph do differently with the next idea?
qa.a: Joseph could pick one idea, set a fixed stretch of time and one measure for it, and tell the team before changing course, so the test can finish.

qa.q: Why might Joseph feel each change was sensible at the time?
qa.a: After each investor chat Joseph had just heard fresh interest, so the newest idea would have looked like the safest bet.

grounding: The note shows a founder redirecting the product after each investor conversation so that nothing is tested long enough to learn from.

subtype: Approach: cutting losses and shutting down cleanly [Revision]
passage:
Subject: Closing the reminder tool, and thank you

Dear Ms Kulkarni,

Pankaj and I ran the tests you suggested for six weeks. We called ninety clinics and got a few polite demos, and not one asked to pay. We sat with that on Sunday and agreed to close, so I wanted you to hear it from me first.

On Monday we refunded every advance payment, all fourteen of them. Today we send our users a thank-you note. Our codebase notes, with what we tried and what failed, go into a shared folder that anyone can read.

I am sad, honestly, but there is relief too, and mostly gratitude for the time you gave us. We hope to ask for your advice again on whatever comes next.

Warm regards,
Gautam

qa.q: How many advance payments did Gautam and Pankaj refund?
qa.a: They refunded all fourteen advance payments.

qa.q: How does Gautam feel about closing the company?
qa.a: Gautam feels sad but also relieved and grateful, saying so plainly in the closing lines.

qa.q: What other approach could the founders have tried before closing, and why?
qa.a: They could have interviewed the clinics that said no to find the root cause, which might have shown a fixable problem, though six weeks of tests already gave a clear answer.

qa.q: How might the users who paid in advance see the way the company closed?
qa.a: They get their money back and a thank-you, so they are more likely to trust Gautam and Pankaj on a future venture. 🙂

grounding: The email shows founders ending the product after tests show no demand, refunding customers, thanking users and sharing notes.

passage:
Day one, Tuesday. The course sold to students in ones and twos, and the sales chart was flat. "We keep asking why students won't pay," Divyansh said, tapping the marker on the desk. "Wrong question. Who is better off when a student learns this?" Shalini leaned in and started a list: exam-coaching centres, schools, parents' groups.
Day four. Divyansh phoned a coaching centre owner and asked about the centre's weakest subject. It happened to be the topic the team's videos already covered.
Day seventeen. The centre bought 150 seats for its batch. The videos did not change at all; only the person the team talked to did.

qa.q: How many seats did the coaching centre buy?
qa.a: The centre bought 150 seats.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when Divyansh asked the new question?
qa.a: Shalini was curious and hopeful: leaning in and starting a list right away shows the question opened something up.

qa.q: What other approach could the team use to check that the new customer is right, and why?
qa.a: They could use time-boxing: set a few weeks and a target number of centres, so a weak result shows quickly instead of dragging on.

qa.q: How might the centre's owner see the offer?
qa.a: The owner sees a fix for the centre's weakest subject that many students can use, which is a different pitch from asking each student to pay.

grounding: The passage shows a team asking who benefits from students learning and taking the same course to a new kind of buyer.

subtype: Approach: explaining the pivot to the team openly [Action]
passage:
On Monday morning Uday pulled the whole team into the meeting room and put a sheet on the wall screen: monthly users, money in, money out, the line going the wrong way. "This is where we are," Uday said. "And this is what I want to change."
Then came a slide for each role. The mobile work would move to a clinic dashboard. Support and sales would sit together. Parul's testing job would grow to cover the new product, with the same pay and a new review date.
Parul asked three questions about the numbers and then nodded slowly. By Friday two engineers had handed in notice, politely and with thanks. Everyone else stayed and started on Monday's plan.

qa.q: What did Uday put on the wall screen at the start of the meeting?
qa.a: Uday put up a sheet of monthly users, money in and money out.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling during the meeting?
qa.a: Parul was wary at first and then steadier: asking three questions about the numbers and then nodding slowly shows the doubts were being answered.

qa.q: What could Uday do to help the two engineers who left?
qa.a: Uday could offer a fair handover period and a reference, so the departure is respectful and the team's work continues smoothly.

qa.q: How might the two engineers who left have seen the meeting?
qa.a: They probably respected the openness even though the new plan was not for them, since they left politely and with thanks.

grounding: The passage shows a founder sharing the numbers, reasons and each role's future openly, so that most of the team commits despite two departures.

subtype: Approach: avoiding the data until forced [Pitfall]
passage:
I sit two desks from Hafsa in a shared office, so I see the Monday routine. The dashboard tab stays shut. Hafsa opens a design tool, refills the water bottle, answers messages. Once I joked, "Have you looked at the numbers?" and got a bright "Later!" I felt uneasy but didn't push.
This month a letter from the bank arrived. Hafsa read it standing up, sat down slowly, and finally opened the dashboard. I glimpsed a line sloping down for four months. Hafsa said only, "Okay," and cancelled the planned hire. I can't say whether it was fear or plain exhaustion I was watching.
By evening there was one cheaper plan left on the notepad.
— Nandini

qa.q: How long had the line on the dashboard been sloping down?
qa.a: It had been sloping down for four months.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have been feeling each Monday while keeping the dashboard tab shut?
qa.a: Probably dread about the numbers, though Nandini cannot be sure: the closed tab and the bright "Later!" suggest Hafsa was steering away from something painful.

qa.q: What could Hafsa have done differently on those Mondays?
qa.a: Hafsa could have looked at the numbers for a few minutes each week with someone supportive, so a slow slide would show up while there were still several options.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini to watch a desk neighbour avoid the numbers?
qa.a: Nandini feels uneasy and unsure, wanting to say more but not wanting to push, so the joke was as far as it went.

grounding: The account shows a founder skipping the dashboard weekly until the bank forces a look, by which time the decline is long and choices are fewer.

passage:
Anders put two coffees on the table in the Malmö co-working kitchen. "You have said no to investors four times," he said. "Help me understand why staying small matters so much."
Ivan turned the cup. "If someone else sits on our board, they may start deciding what we build. I started this to choose our own product."
"Okay. Mine is the rival's launch in spring. If we're slow, the window closes and there is nothing left to be in control of."
Ivan was quiet, then laughed a little. "So you don't need the money, you need speed. And I don't need to stay poor, I need to keep the say."
They took a marker and wrote three options on the glass: a small round with no board seat, a bank loan for one hire, or nothing.

qa.q: Where were the two co-founders when they talked?
qa.a: They were in the co-working kitchen in Malmö.

qa.q: What is Ivan afraid of, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ivan fears losing control of the product, shown in the line about someone else sitting on the board and deciding what gets built.

qa.q: What could the two do next to test which option fits both worries?
qa.a: They could set a short deadline to price each of the three options on the glass against the spring launch and against who would control the product.

qa.q: How might Anders have seen Ivan's refusals before the coffee talk?
qa.a: Before the talk, Anders probably saw them as stubbornness that risked the spring window; afterwards they looked like a fear about control.

grounding: The passage shows co-founders asking why behind their opposite positions and finding a fear of losing control and a fear of missing the market window.

subtype: Approach: writing down roles and decision rights [Action]
passage:
After the second hard argument about the stitching unit, Dilnaz and Afreen sat on the back step of the shop in their small town, a pot of chai between them. "Let's write it down," Afreen said, and pulled out a page from the ledger.
They listed the decisions one by one. Afreen would choose designs and colours. Dilnaz would hire and let people go. Any spend above five thousand rupees needed both of them. They signed the bottom and pinned it above the cutting table.
Two weeks later they disagreed about hiring a second tailor. Dilnaz pointed at the page. Afreen read it, sighed, and said, "Fine, that one is yours, but tell me before you decide."
The kettle went back on.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz and Afreen pin the signed page?
qa.a: They pinned it above the cutting table.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when the page pointed to Dilnaz for the hiring decision?
qa.a: Afreen felt a flash of irritation that softened into acceptance, shown by the sigh, the "Fine" and the request to be told first.

qa.q: What could the two add if the page does not cover a new kind of dispute?
qa.a: They could add the new topic to the page after talking calmly, and sign the new line again so both agree on who decides.

qa.q: How might a new tailor see the page above the cutting table?
qa.a: A new tailor can see who decides what, so knows whom to ask and does not get caught between two bosses.

grounding: The passage shows co-founders writing down who decides what and checking a later disagreement against the signed page.

subtype: Approach: avoiding the conflict to keep peace [Pitfall]
passage:
Wednesday, late.
I blew up today. On the client call, in the shared chat, I typed: "Some of us actually deliver on time." Everyone saw it. Seema's camera went off. The client asked, very politely, if we could reschedule.
The thing is, I have said nothing since March. Not about the logo files, not about the report, not about the demo that slid twice. Every time I told myself it wasn't worth a fight and we should keep the peace. My hands were shaking as I typed, and part of me wanted it to hurt.
Now Seema won't answer my messages, the client is unsure of us, and the real problem is still not discussed.
Tomorrow I owe an apology for how I said it.
— Pankaj

qa.q: Where did Pankaj type the angry message?
qa.a: Pankaj typed it in the shared chat during the client call.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling just before typing the message?
qa.a: Pankaj was full of built-up resentment: months of silence, shaking hands and wanting the message to hurt show it.

qa.q: What could Pankaj have done earlier instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Pankaj could have raised one missed deadline privately soon after it happened, in calm words, so the problem stayed small.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt when the message appeared in front of the client?
qa.a: Seema was probably embarrassed and hurt, since the first sign of any problem came in public; the camera going off hints at it, though it is not proof.

grounding: The diary shows a founder keeping quiet about a partner's late work until resentment bursts out in a message during a client call.

passage:
I'm Meera, the junior analyst, and I saw the pricing fight from my desk. Francis arrived Monday with screenshots of three competitors' price pages. Deepak came Tuesday with a survey sheet and a folder of quotes. By Thursday they were quoting each other's old mistakes, and the price hardly came up.
On Friday Deepak said, "Fine, your number," and shut the laptop. Francis told me afterwards it was good to have it settled.
Since then, in the stand-ups, Deepak just says "nothing from me". I can't tell if that's hurt or just tiredness. Last week I found a half-written plan for a simpler free trial in a shared folder, dated before the pricing fight. Nobody had seen it.
— Meera

qa.q: What did Deepak bring to the discussion on Tuesday?
qa.a: Deepak brought a survey sheet and a folder of quotes.

qa.q: What might Deepak be feeling since giving in on the price?
qa.a: Deepak may be hurt, shown by the flat "nothing from me" in stand-ups, though Meera admits it could be tiredness.

qa.q: What could the founders try next time they disagree about a price?
qa.a: They could agree on what evidence would settle it and run a small test of both prices, so the question is about the customers rather than who is right.

qa.q: Why might Francis feel the debate went well?
qa.a: Francis got a decision and a settled question, and told Meera that was good, without seeing what it cost in Deepak's ideas.

grounding: The account shows two founders gathering proof to win a pricing argument, after which the one who lost stops sharing ideas.
